verdict: Recommended: LS_short_w_st10_2 — the hardened long book (20% position cap, halve-at-10% / pause-at-15% drawdown rule) plus a weekly short book in NIFTY 200 names. NIFTY 500: 16.6% CAGR, −29% max drawdown (Sa15d9d9c: 18.0% / −46%). Other universes: 9.1–12.1% CAGR with −15% to −22% drawdowns.

The drawdown rule did most of the work, not the shorts: on its own it cut Sa15d9d9c's NIFTY 500 drawdown from −46% to −32% at the same 18.0% CAGR (L_dd). The short book took a further 3 points off the drawdown and softened 2008 and 2018–20.

The short book alone makes about nothing: its 6% CAGR is the liquid-fund interest on idle cash. It earns in bear markets (over Aug 2018 – Aug 2020, including cash: +23% to +33% for the monthly versions, +11% to +22% for the weekly ones; +24% to +27% in 2008 for the weekly trend-exit versions) and bleeds slowly otherwise. That is insurance, which is what it is for.

The NIFTY-futures hedge is a fair alternative: LS_hedge100 had the smallest 2008 loss (−8%), but cost about 1 point of CAGR; a 50% hedge sat in between. Shorting individual weak stocks did slightly better overall and is the better complement in mid/small-cap bear markets such as 2018–20.
part1: The drawdown rule (L_dd) is the single best change: same 18.0% on NIFTY 500, drawdown −46% → −32%, 2018–20 loss −44% → −29%.
Position caps cost CAGR (15%: −2 points; 20%: −1.3; 25%: −1.1) and barely cut the drawdown on their own: big winners are where the money is. A cap is still worth having as a concentration rule.
0.75% risk with the cap and drawdown rule (L_cap20_dd_r075) is the most conservative version: 15.2% / −26% on NIFTY 500 and −14% to −22% elsewhere.

Risk ladder on L_cap20_dd (Sde394f26): 0.25% risk (Se01037f3) 11.7% / −13% on NIFTY 500; 0.5% (S150d745e) 13.8% / −19%; 0.75% (S9f9bd8e9) 15.2% / −26%; 1% 16.6% / −32%. Drawdown falls faster than CAGR. At 0.25% only 10–23% of capital is invested on average, so much of the return is the liquid-fund rate. 0.5% is the recommended level: 8.5–13.8% CAGR, −11% to −21% drawdowns across the 5 universes.
part2: The exact monthly mirror fires rarely (30 trades in 26 years): stocks in downtrends seldom become overbought on a monthly chart. Weekly signals give 90–100 trades.
Every short version has a low win rate (20–42%): shorts in a rising market get stopped often; the payoff comes from a few bear phases.
Shorting without the NIFTY 200-DMA filter (S_w_nomkt) or with only weekly/daily trend filters (S_w_wd) doubles the trades and the drawdown: shorting in bull markets is a losing game in India.

Short-side figures assume futures are available on every NIFTY 200 name since 2001. In reality single-stock futures began in Nov 2001 on a short list that grew over time; the 2002–07 short trades are optimistic.
part3: Adding either short book cut the NIFTY 500 drawdown from −32% to −28%/−29% with no CAGR cost; on the other universes, drawdowns stayed the same or improved slightly.
The 8% total-open-risk cap never came into play (identical results): with 1% risk per trade and stops trailed, open risk stayed below 8%.
Combining shorts with a 50% NIFTY hedge cut 2008 further but cost 0.1–0.4 points of CAGR; not worth the complexity.
risk: Short-side mechanics in real life: stock futures have lot sizes (₹5–10 lakh notional), so with small capital the short book cannot be sized at 1% risk; the NIFTY futures hedge (or NIFTY puts) is the practical form below ₹50 lakh capital.
Gaps and circuits hurt shorts more: results days, upper circuits and short squeezes are only partly captured (stops fill at the open on gaps). Keep shorts out of results weeks.
Margin: 25% of notional is assumed; SEBI peak-margin rules and volatility can push it higher, which ties up more cash.

All universes are today's constituents (survivorship bias): it flatters longs and hurts shorts (failed stocks that would have been good shorts are missing). The true short-side value is likely somewhat higher than shown.
Next step: paper-trade LS_short_w_st10_2 alongside S7c315ace for 6 months; journal every signal, including those skipped for lot size or margin.
part4: NIFTY 750 at 1% risk (Sde394f26): 19.8% / −30% against 16.6% / −32% on NIFTY 500. 86 of 670 trades were microcaps and made 14% of the profit; most of the advantage came after 2019 (26.7% vs 18.6%), only +1.3 points before.
Heavier microcap slippage barely matters: 0.5% per side costs 0.4 points (19.4%), 1% costs 0.7 (19.1%). Trades are held for months, so entry/exit costs are small next to the moves.

A liquidity floor removes the whole microcap advantage: with a 60-day median traded value of at least ₹2 crore, NIFTY 750 makes 13.9% and NIFTY 500 13.8%; at ₹5 crore, 11.0% and 10.9%. The extra return came from stocks too thin to trade in size at the time.

The floor also cuts NIFTY 500 hard, mostly before 2019 (15.7% → 7.8% at ₹5 crore). Part of that is a flaw of a fixed rupee floor: ₹5 crore a day in 2003 was a large stock, so the filter removes most of the early universe. But it also shows that much of the early return came from stocks that were small and illiquid then and became large later — the survivorship effect again.

Verdict: keep NIFTY 500 as the universe. NIFTY 750's extra return does not survive a liquidity requirement. A fairer next test is a floor that scales with the market (e.g. top 60% of the universe by traded value each day).
